title: Aper Calydonius. Meleager
titleEn: The Quarrel and the Brand — Metamorphoses VIII.403–546
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The boar is brought down, and Meleager gives the hide and the tusked head to Atalanta; his mother's brothers snatch the prize back, and he kills them both. Althaea — sister to the dead men, mother to their killer — is left holding the brand the Fates laid on the fire at his birth, when they gave the wood and the child one span of days. She burns it; he dies far off of a fire he cannot see; she takes her own life, and Latona's daughter turns his mourning sisters into birds at his tomb. The centre of the part is her long deliberation, in which the two names inside her fight it out.

sentences.t:
Ibat in adversum proles Ixionis hostem
Pirithous valida quatiens venabula dextra.
sentences.l: Against the enemy facing him was going Ixion's offspring, Pirithous, brandishing his hunting-spears in his strong right hand.
sentences.i: Ixion's son Pirithous went straight at the beast that faced him, shaking his hunting-spears in his powerful right hand.
sentences.n: proles Ixionis, “Ixion's offspring”, is patronymic periphrasis: Pirithous, king of the Lapiths and Theseus' inseparable companion. in adversum ... hostem is the enemy standing opposite, face to face; hostis, the ordinary word for a war-enemy, is used of the boar throughout this fight, and comes again at 418.

sentences.t:
Cui “procul” Aegides “o me mihi carior” inquit
“pars animae consiste meae! licet eminus esse
fortibus: Ancaeo nocuit temeraria virtus.”
sentences.l: To him “At a distance,” says the son of Aegeus, “O dearer to me than myself, part of my own soul, take your stand! It is permitted to the brave to be far off: reckless valour did harm to Ancaeus.”
sentences.i: “Keep back,” Theseus said to him. “You who are dearer to me than I am to myself, part of my own soul — stand there! The brave are allowed to fight at long range: it was reckless courage that harmed Ancaeus.”
sentences.n: Aegides, “son of Aegeus”, is Theseus. Cui is a dative with inquit, “says to him”, thrown to the head of the line so the speech can start at once. licet takes a dative of the person and an infinitive: “it is permitted to the brave to be at a distance”. Ancaeus is named again at 519.

sentences.t: Dixit et aerata torsit grave cuspide cornum.
sentences.l: He spoke, and hurled the cornel-wood, heavy with its bronze-shod point.
sentences.i: He spoke, and sent the cornel shaft flying, weighted with its point of bronze.
sentences.n: cornum, cornel-wood, stands for the spear made of it — the material named instead of the weapon. torqueo is the regular verb for launching a spear with a twist of the arm. aerata cuspide goes with grave as an ablative of cause: the shaft is heavy by reason of the bronze on its end.

sentences.t:
Quo bene librato votique potente futuro,
obstitit abscisa frondosus ab arbore ramus.
sentences.l: And when this had been well poised and was about to be master of its wish, a leafy branch from a lopped tree stood in the way.
sentences.i: It was well aimed and would have had its wish, but a leafy bough from a pruned tree got in its path.
sentences.n: quo bene librato ... potente futuro is an ablative absolute — a self-contained “with X in such a state” phrase where English wants a clause — and it opens with a connecting relative, quo meaning “and this”, a very common way for a Latin sentence to hook onto the one before. voti potens is an idiom, “in possession of one's prayer”, so “about to get what it asked for”. Magnus prints abscisa, “cut back, lopped”; some editions print aesculea, “of oak”.

sentences.t:
Misit et Aesonides iaculum: quod casus ab illo
vertit in inmeriti fatum latrantis et inter
ilia coniectum tellure per ilia fixum est.
sentences.l: The son of Aeson too let fly a javelin: which chance turned away from that beast into the doom of an undeserving barker, and, hurled between the flanks, it was fixed in the earth through the flanks.
sentences.i: Jason threw his javelin too, and chance turned it from the boar to the death of an innocent hound: it went in between the dog's flanks, through them, and pinned it to the ground.
sentences.n: Aesonides, “son of Aeson”, is Jason. latrantis, “of the barking one”, is a present participle used as a noun for a hound, and inmeriti says the animal had done nothing to earn this. The edition prints ilia twice in consecutive clauses, inter ilia and per ilia; the repetition stands in the transmitted text and is left exactly as the edition has it.

sentences.t:
At manus Oenidae variat, missisque duabus
hasta prior terra, medio stetit altera tergo.
sentences.l: But the hand of Oeneus' son varies: with two spears having been thrown, the first stood in the ground, the other in the middle of the back.
sentences.i: But the hand of Oeneus' son had mixed results: of the two spears he threw, the first stuck in the earth, the second in the middle of the boar's back.
sentences.n: Oenides, “son of Oeneus”, is Meleager, who is not named outright until 515. missis duabus is an ablative absolute with hastis understood from hasta in the next line. Notice the present variat beside the perfect stetit: Ovid slides between historic present and perfect all through this narrative, bringing one action close and setting the other at a distance.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, dum saevit, dum corpora versat in orbem
stridentemque novo spumam cum sanguine fundit,
vulneris auctor adest hostemque inritat ad iram
splendidaque adversos venabula condit in armos.
sentences.l: No delay: while the beast rages, while it wheels its body about in a circle and pours out hissing foam with fresh blood, the author of the wound is there, and goads his enemy to fury, and buries his gleaming hunting-spears in the shoulders facing him.
sentences.i: There was no pause. While the boar raged, spinning round and pouring out hissing foam mixed with fresh blood, the man who had wounded it closed in, provoked it to fury, and drove his bright spear into the shoulders it turned toward him.
sentences.n: nec mora is a stock narrative formula, “no delay”, used to jam two actions together. corpora is a poetic plural for the one body, a licence the hexameter takes freely and one you will meet constantly. vulneris auctor, “the author of the wound”, is another periphrasis for Meleager, and auctor comes back in a far darker sense at 449 and 493.

sentences.t:
Gaudia testantur socii clamore secundo
victricemque petunt dextrae coniungere dextram
inmanemque ferum multa tellure iacentem
mirantes spectant, neque adhuc contingere tutum
esse putant; sed tela tamen sua quisque cruentat.
sentences.l: His comrades bear witness to their joy with an approving shout, and seek to join the victorious right hand to their own right hand, and gazing in wonder they look at the monstrous beast lying over a great stretch of ground, and they think it not yet safe to touch him; but each man bloodies his own weapon all the same.
sentences.i: His companions declared their delight with an answering cheer and pressed to take the victorious right hand in their own. They stared in wonder at the huge beast sprawled over a wide stretch of ground, still thinking it unsafe to touch him — and yet every one of them reddened his own weapon in it.
sentences.n: clamore secundo is the shout of assent that follows a success; secundus is “favouring” before it is “second”. multa tellure measures the animal by the ground it covers. The last clause is the whole quarrel in advance: each man dips his weapon in the dead boar so as to have a claim on the kill.

sentences.t:
Ipse pede imposito caput exitiabile pressit
atque ita “sume mei spolium, Nonacria, iuris,”
dixit “et in partem veniat mea gloria tecum.”
sentences.l: He himself, with his foot placed on it, pressed down the deadly head, and thus he said: “Take the spoil that is of my right, Nonacrian, and let my glory come into a share with you.”
sentences.i: He set his own foot on the deadly head and bore it down, and said: “Take the spoil that is mine by right, girl of Nonacris, and let my glory come to be shared with you.”
sentences.n: pede imposito is another ablative absolute. Nonacria names Atalanta by her home, Nonacris in Arcadia: a place-adjective used as a vocative for the person is ordinary epic manners. mei ... iuris is a possessive genitive with spolium, “spoil belonging to my right”, and in partem venire has a legal ring — to come into a share.

sentences.t:
Protinus exuvias rigidis horrentia saetis
terga dat et magnis insignia dentibus ora.
sentences.l: At once he gives the spoils: the back bristling with stiff bristles, and the head marked out by its great tusks.
sentences.i: At once he handed over the trophies — the hide with its stiff bristles standing up, and the head distinguished by its great tusks.
sentences.n: terga and ora stand in apposition to exuvias, naming the two pieces the spoils are made of; both are poetic plurals for one back and one head (compare corpora at 416). rigidis saetis with horrentia and magnis dentibus with insignia are ablatives of means: bristling by reason of the bristles, marked out by the tusks.

sentences.t:
Illi laetitiae est cum munere muneris auctor:
invidere alii, totoque erat agmine murmur.
sentences.l: To her the giver of the gift is a joy along with the gift: the others envied, and through the whole company there was a muttering.
sentences.i: The gift pleased her, and so did the giver; the rest were jealous, and a muttering ran through the whole company.
sentences.n: illi ... laetitiae est is the double dative: a dative of the person with a predicative dative of the effect, “is for a joy to her”. invidere is the poetic third-plural perfect for inviderunt — the ending -ere for -erunt is everywhere in hexameter verse, and it returns at 452 and 456.

sentences.t:
E quibus ingenti tendentes bracchia voce
“pone age nec titulos intercipe, femina, nostros,”
Thestiadae clamant “nec te fiducia formae
decipiat, ne sit longe tibi captus amore
auctor” et huic adimunt munus, ius muneris illi.
sentences.l: Out of their number, stretching out their arms, with a huge voice the sons of Thestius shout: “Put it down, come now, and do not intercept our honours, woman, and do not let confidence in your beauty deceive you, lest the giver, caught by love, be far from you” — and from her they take the gift, from him the right to give it.
sentences.i: Out of the crowd the sons of Thestius flung out their arms and shouted at the top of their voices: “Put it down, and stop stealing the credit that is ours, woman; and do not let confidence in your looks mislead you — the man who gave it is in love with you, and may be a long way off when you need him.” And they took the gift from her and the right of giving from him.
sentences.n: Thestiadae are Plexippus and Toxeus, sons of Thestius, named at 440 and 441; they are Althaea's brothers, and so Meleager's uncles. titulos are the marks of honour a victory earns, the word used of an inscription cut on a monument. femina in the vocative is not neutral address here — it is thrown at her as her whole disqualification, and the English keeps the sneer. ne sit longe ... auctor is a clause of warning, and the warning is a threat: he will not be near enough to protect her.

sentences.t:
Non tulit et tumida frendens Mavortius ira
“discite, raptores alieni” dixit “honoris,
facta minis quantum distent,” hausitque nefando
pectora Plexippi nil tale timentia ferro.
sentences.l: He did not bear it, and grinding his teeth in swollen anger the son of Mars said: “Learn, you robbers of another's honour, how far deeds stand apart from threats” — and with unspeakable steel he drained the breast of Plexippus, fearing nothing of the kind.
sentences.i: Meleager would not put up with it. Grinding his teeth in swelling rage, the man of Mars' blood said: “Learn, you thieves of another man's honour, how far deeds stand from threats” — and with abominable steel he ran Plexippus through the chest; he had feared nothing of the sort.
sentences.n: Mavortius, “of Mars”, is an epithet for Meleager: one version of the story makes Mars his father. haurio of a weapon is to sink it in and draw it out again, literally “drain”. pectora is once more the poetic plural, and nil tale timentia is a participle agreeing with it, “fearing nothing of the kind”. nefando, “not to be spoken of”, is the narrator's judgment on the act rather than the speaker's: this is the killing of kin.

sentences.t:
Toxea, quid faciat, dubium pariterque volentem
ulcisci fratrem fraternaque fata timentem
haud patitur dubitare diu calidumque priori
caede recalfecit consorti sanguine telum.
sentences.l: Toxeus, doubtful what he was to do and equally wanting to avenge his brother and fearing his brother's fate, he does not suffer to hesitate long; and the blade still warm from the earlier slaughter he warmed again with kindred blood.
sentences.i: Toxeus was in doubt what to do, wanting alike to avenge his brother and dreading his brother's fate; Meleager did not let him hesitate long, and warmed the blade, still hot from the first killing, over again in blood of his own stock.
sentences.n: Toxea is the accusative of Toxeus, keeping the Greek ending -a where Latin would have -um; it is the object of patitur. quid faciat is a deliberative subjunctive inside an indirect question, “what he was to do”. ulcisci is the infinitive of the deponent ulciscor, passive in form but active in meaning, “to avenge”. consorti sanguine is blood that shares one lot, blood of a single family: through Althaea it is Meleager's own.

sentences.t:
Dona deum templis nato victore ferebat,
cum videt exstinctos fratres Althaea referri.
sentences.l: She was carrying gifts to the temples of the gods, her son being the victor, when Althaea sees her brothers brought back dead.
sentences.i: Althaea was carrying offerings to the temples of the gods because her son had won, when she saw her brothers being carried home dead.
sentences.n: deum is the shortened genitive plural for deorum, normal in verse. nato victore is an ablative absolute built of two nouns with no participle at all — Latin has no present participle of esse, so “her son being victor” has to be made this way, and English wants “because her son had won”. The imperfect ferebat sets the scene and the present videt cuts across it: the historic present again, as at 414.

sentences.t:
Quae plangore dato maestis clamoribus urbem
implet et auratis mutavit vestibus atras.
sentences.l: And she — with lamentation raised — fills the city with mourning cries, and changed her gilded robes for black ones.
sentences.i: She raised the death-wail, filled the city with cries of mourning, and changed her gold-embroidered robes for black.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative, “and she”, the same hook as quo at 409. plangore dato is an ablative absolute; plangor is the ritual beating of the breast that opens a Roman mourning. In mutavit auratis vestibus atras the accusative atras, with vestes understood, is what she puts on and the ablative names what she gives up — she had dressed for a thanksgiving.

sentences.t:
At simul est auctor necis editus, excidit omnis
luctus et a lacrimis in poenae versus amorem est.
sentences.l: But as soon as the author of the killing was made known, all grief fell away and was turned from tears into a love of punishment.
sentences.i: But the moment the killer's name came out, her grief fell away entirely and turned from tears to a hunger for vengeance.
sentences.n: simul here stands for simul ac, “as soon as”. editus est of a name is “brought out, published”. poenae amorem is an objective genitive of an unsettling kind: what she now loves is the punishing itself. auctor necis answers vulneris auctor at 418 — the same word, and now it means her son.

sentences.t:
Stipes erat, quem, cum partus enixa iaceret
Thestias, in flammam triplices posuere sorores;
staminaque impresso fatalia pollice nentes
“tempora” dixerunt “eadem lignoque tibique,
sentences.l: There was a log which, when the daughter of Thestius lay there, her child brought forth, the three sisters set in the flame; and, spinning the threads of fate with thumb pressed upon them, they said: “The same span of time, to the wood and to you,
sentences.i: There was a log which the three sisters had laid on the fire while the daughter of Thestius lay in childbed, her child just delivered; and as they spun the threads of fate under the pressure of their thumbs they said: “One and the same span of time, to this wood and to you,
sentences.n: Thestias, “the daughter of Thestius”, is Althaea, named by the same father who gave her brothers their name at 434. triplices sorores are the Parcae, the three Fates. partus enixa is a perfect participle of the deponent enitor, active in meaning, “having brought forth her offspring”. posuere is the -ere perfect again (see 431), and impresso pollice is an ablative absolute describing the thumb pressed to the thread as it is drawn out. The verb of the Fates' own sentence, damus, is held over to the next line.

sentences.t:
o modo nate, damus.” Quo postquam carmine dicto
excessere deae, flagrantem mater ab igne
eripuit ramum sparsitque liquentibus undis.
sentences.l: child but now born, we give.” After which spell had been spoken and the goddesses had gone out, the mother snatched the blazing branch from the fire and sprinkled it with running water.
sentences.i: child new-born, we give.” When that charm had been uttered and the goddesses were gone, the mother snatched the burning brand out of the fire and doused it with running water.
sentences.n: quo ... carmine dicto is another ablative absolute opening with a connecting relative, quo meaning “and this”. carmen is not merely a song but a binding formula, a spell: what the Fates say has the force of law. excessere is the -ere perfect once more. sparsit ... undis, “sprinkled with waters”, is understatement for putting the fire out.

sentences.t:
Ille diu fuerat penetralibus abditus imis
servatusque tuos, iuvenis, servaverat annos.
sentences.l: It had long been hidden away in the innermost recesses, and, kept safe, it had kept safe your years, young man.
sentences.i: For years it lay hidden in the deepest part of the house; being preserved, it had preserved your life, young man.
sentences.n: tuos, iuvenis — the narrator breaks off from telling and addresses Meleager directly. This is apostrophe, and its effect is to set the audience beside a character at the moment of his ruin. penetralia are the innermost rooms of a house, where the household gods stand. servatus ... servaverat sets the passive participle against the active pluperfect of one verb: the log's safety and the man's are a single fact.

sentences.t:
Protulit hunc genetrix taedasque et fragmina poni
imperat et positis inimicos admovet ignes.
sentences.l: The mother brought it out and orders pine-torches and splinters to be laid down, and to the pile so laid she brings up hostile fire.
sentences.i: His mother brought it out, ordered pine brands and kindling to be piled up, and set enemy fire to the pile.
sentences.n: poni is a passive infinitive in indirect command after imperat. positis, the perfect participle of the same verb, stands as a noun, “to the things laid down”. inimicos ignes — the fire is called hostile because of what it is for; the adjective belongs to the deed rather than to the flame, a transfer Latin makes easily.

sentences.t:
Tum conata quater flammis imponere ramum,
coepta quater tenuit. Pugnant materque sororque,
et diversa trahunt unum duo nomina pectus.
sentences.l: Then, four times having tried to lay the branch on the flames, four times she checked what she had begun. The mother and the sister fight, and two opposed names drag one heart.
sentences.i: Four times she made to lay the branch on the fire, and four times she stopped herself. Mother and sister were at war in her, and two names at odds dragged one heart two different ways.
sentences.n: conata is from the deponent conor, passive in form and active in meaning, “having tried” (compare ulcisci at 442). coepta, “the things begun”, is a neuter plural participle standing as a noun. materque sororque are not two women but two roles inside one woman: she is Meleager's mother and the dead men's sister at once. diversa is neuter plural agreeing with duo nomina — the two names are set against each other — and the force of the line is its arithmetic, two names dragging one heart. Magnus prints the plural Pugnant, with mater and soror as joint subjects; some editions print the singular pugnat.

sentences.t:
Saepe metu sceleris pallebant ora futuri,
saepe suum fervens oculis dabat ira ruborem.
sentences.l: Often her face grew pale with fear of the crime to come; often her boiling anger gave its own redness to her eyes.
sentences.i: Again and again her face went white with dread of the crime ahead; again and again her seething rage put its own flush into her eyes.
sentences.n: ora is a poetic plural for her one face (see 416). sceleris futuri is a genitive after metu, “fear of the crime that was to be” — she is already calling it a crime. The balanced saepe clauses set pallor against flush: the fight named at 463 is showing on the outside.

sentences.t:
Et modo nescio quid similis crudele minanti
vultus erat, modo quem misereri credere posses.
sentences.l: And at one moment her face was like that of one threatening some cruel thing or other; at another, like one whom you could have believed to be pitying.
sentences.i: One moment her look was that of a woman threatening something cruel; the next, of a woman you would have sworn was full of pity.
sentences.n: nescio quid is a frozen phrase meaning “something or other”, taking crudele with it; it is not an indirect question and nescio is not being conjugated. similis governs the dative minanti. credere posses is a potential subjunctive with the generalising second person, “you could have believed” — the reader is set in front of her face and made to guess.

sentences.t:
Cumque ferus lacrimas animi siccaverat ardor,
inveniebantur lacrimae tamen. Utque carina,
sentences.l: And when the fierce burning of her spirit had dried her tears, tears were found all the same. And as a keel,
sentences.i: And whenever the fierce heat of her spirit had dried her tears up, still more tears were found. As a ship's hull,
sentences.n: cum with the pluperfect indicative here is iterative, “whenever”, and the imperfect inveniebantur answers it: this happened over and over. ferus ardor treats her rage as literal heat, hot enough to evaporate tears. The sentence breaks off at the line-end into a simile that runs to 472 and is turned back on her at 473.

sentences.t:
quam ventus ventoque rapit contrarius aestus,
vim geminam sentit paretque incerta duobus:
Thestias haud aliter dubiis adfectibus errat
inque vices ponit positamque resuscitat iram.
sentences.l: which the wind and a tide running against the wind sweep along, feels the twofold force and, uncertain, obeys them both: not otherwise does the daughter of Thestius drift among wavering passions, and by turns lays her anger down and wakes it again once laid down.
sentences.i: driven by the wind and by a tide that runs against the wind, feels the double force and, unsure, gives way to both — just so Althaea drifted among her wavering feelings, laying her anger down and, once it was down, rousing it again by turns.
sentences.n: carina, the keel, stands for the whole ship. haud aliter, “not otherwise”, is the standard formula that brings an epic simile back to its subject. in vices is “by turns”. ponit ... positam ... resuscitat plays the participle back against the verb: the anger she has just put down is the very thing she takes up again.

sentences.t:
Incipit esse tamen melior germana parente,
et consanguineas ut sanguine leniat umbras,
impietate pia est. Nam postquam pestifer ignis
convaluit, “rogus iste cremet mea viscera” dixit.
sentences.l: Yet she begins to be better as a sister than as a parent, and, so that she may soothe with blood the shades that share her blood, she is dutiful by undutifulness. For after the plague-bearing fire had gathered strength, “Let that pyre burn my own flesh,” she said.
sentences.i: Still, the sister in her began to outdo the mother, and, to appease with blood the shades that were her own blood, she was loyal by an act of disloyalty. When the deadly fire had taken hold she said: “Let that pyre burn my own flesh.”
sentences.n: melior ... parente is an ablative of comparison: better in the one role than in the other, not better than some other person. impietate pia est turns on pietas, the Roman duty owed to family and gods — she discharges it by breaking it, and the two words are set side by side so the contradiction cannot be missed. consanguineas ... sanguine repeats the root: blood-sharing shades, appeased with blood. viscera is the inward parts, and of a mother's child her own flesh; the word returns at 516 and 532.

sentences.t:
Utque manu dira lignum fatale tenebat,
ante sepulcrales infelix adstitit aras
sentences.l: And as she held the wood of fate in her dreadful hand, the ill-starred woman took her stand before the altars of the tomb.
sentences.i: Holding the doom-laden wood in her terrible hand, she stood — poor woman — before the altars of the dead.
sentences.n: dira belongs by sense to what the hand is about to do rather than to the hand itself; Latin shifts an adjective onto a neighbouring noun like this constantly. infelix used on its own of a person is the narrator's pity, “the doomed woman”. sepulcrales arae are altars set up for offerings to the dead, not to the gods above.

sentences.t:
“poenarum” que “deae triplices, furialibus,” inquit,
“Eumenides, sacris vultus advertite vestros.
sentences.l: “Threefold goddesses of punishments,” she says, “Eumenides, turn your faces toward these rites of the Furies.
sentences.i: “Threefold goddesses of retribution — Eumenides — turn your gaze on rites that are the Furies' own.
sentences.n: The Eumenides, “the Kindly Ones”, are the Furies called by the name that placates them. deae triplices deliberately echoes the triplices sorores of 452, so that one set of three answers the other. furialibus sacris is a dative with advertite, “turn toward”. Note the edition's habit, when a speech is broken around inquit, of printing the enclitic outside the quotation: “poenarum” que.

sentences.t:
Ulciscor facioque nefas: mors morte pianda est,
in scelus addendum scelus est, in funera funus.
Per coacervatos pereat domus impia luctus.
sentences.l: I take vengeance and I commit an abomination: death must be atoned for by death, crime must be added onto crime, funeral onto funerals. Through griefs heaped one on another let this unholy house perish.
sentences.i: I am avenging, and I am committing an abomination. Death must be paid for with death, crime piled on crime, funeral on funeral. Let this unholy house go down under griefs heaped one upon another.
sentences.n: pianda est and addendum est are gerundives of obligation — “must be atoned for”, “must be added”. nefas is the noun belonging to nefando at 439, which was the narrator's word for Meleager's killing; she now uses it of what she is about to do. in scelus and in funera use in of piling one thing on top of another, and the Latin keeps a singular funus against the plural funera. domus impia is her own house, and she puts herself inside the judgment: the crime is unholy precisely because it stays in the family.

sentences.t:
An felix Oeneus nato victore fruetur,
Thestius orbus erit? Melius lugebitis ambo.
sentences.l: Or shall fortunate Oeneus enjoy a victorious son, and Thestius be childless? Better — you two shall both mourn.
sentences.i: Or is Oeneus to be the lucky one, with the joy of a son who won, while Thestius is left with no children? Better that the two of you should both be in mourning.
sentences.n: an introduces an indignant question, “or is it to be that ...”. Oeneus is Meleager's father, the Oeneus of Oenides at 414; Thestius is her own father, who has just lost the two sons of 434. fruetur takes an ablative, nato victore. melius is adverbial with lugebitis: not “you will mourn better” but “better so — you shall both mourn”.

sentences.t:
Vos modo, fraterni manes animaeque recentes,
officium sentite meum magnoque paratas
accipite inferias, uteri mala pignera nostri! —
sentences.l: You only, brotherly shades and souls newly made, feel my duty and receive the offerings to the dead prepared at great cost, the evil pledges of my own womb! —
sentences.i: Only you, my brothers' ghosts, souls newly come, take notice of my duty and accept the offering to the dead that I have made ready at great price: the wicked pledge of my own womb.
sentences.n: inferiae are the offerings made at a tomb to the dead, and magno is an ablative of price, “at great cost”. uteri mala pignera nostri stands in apposition to inferias: the offering is her son. pignus, the pledge given to secure a debt, is the ordinary Latin word for a child, and pignera is plural for the one son, the poetic plural again. The edition marks the turns of this soliloquy with dashes — here, and again at 493, 505 and 508.

sentences.t:
Ei mihi! quo rapior? Fratres, ignoscite matri.
Deficiunt ad coepta manus. Meruisse fatemur
illum, cur pereat: mortis mihi displicet auctor. —
sentences.l: Ah me! where am I being swept? Brothers, forgive a mother. My hands fail at what I began. I confess that he has earned it — a reason why he should die: it is the author of his death that displeases me. —
sentences.i: Oh, where am I being carried? Brothers, forgive a mother. My hands give out at what I have begun. I admit he has earned grounds enough to die — it is the author of his death that I cannot bear.
sentences.n: quo rapior is passive, “where am I being carried off to?”, as if by a current — the same image as the ship at 470–472. fatemur is a plural used by a single speaker of herself. mortis auctor is the third turn of a phrase that has followed the killing right through this part: vulneris auctor at 418, auctor necis at 449, and now the role she is stepping into.

sentences.t:
Ergo impune feret, vivusque et victor et ipso
successu tumidus regnum Calydonis habebit:
vos cinis exiguus gelidaeque iacebitis umbrae?
sentences.l: So then, shall he carry it off unpunished, and alive and victorious and swollen with his very success shall he hold the kingdom of Calydon, while you lie a scanty ash and chill shades?
sentences.i: So he is to get off unpunished, is he — alive, victorious, swollen with his own success, holding the throne of Calydon, while you lie there a little ash and two cold ghosts?
sentences.n: impune ferre is an idiom, “to carry it off without paying”. tumidus is the word used of Meleager's own anger at 437, tumida ira, and she turns it back on him. cinis exiguus is singular and gelidae umbrae plural, both standing as predicates to the plural iacebitis: what is left of the two of them is a little ash and a pair of shades.

sentences.t:
Haud equidem patiar. Pereat sceleratus et ille
spemque patris regnumque trahat patriaeque ruinam.
sentences.l: I shall not allow it, indeed. Let him perish, the criminal, and let him drag down his father's hope and the kingdom and the ruin of his fatherland.
sentences.i: No — I will not have it. Let the criminal die, and drag down with him his father's hope, the throne, and his country in ruins.
sentences.n: pereat and trahat are jussive subjunctives, “let him die”, “let him drag”. sceleratus is “stained with crime”, and it is her word for her own son. et ille, “he too”, sets him alongside the brothers who have already perished. trahere is what a falling thing does to whatever hangs on it; the third object, ruinam, is not something that comes down with him but the ruin he brings, so the one verb has to stretch to cover all three.

sentences.t:
Mens ubi materna est? Ubi sunt pia iura parentum
et quos sustinui bis mensum quinque labores?
sentences.l: Where is a mother's mind? Where are the dutiful claims of parents, and the labours I bore through twice five months?
sentences.i: Where has a mother's heart gone? Where are the sacred claims of a parent, and the pains I carried for ten months together?
sentences.n: mensum is the older genitive plural for mensium. bis quinque mensum is the Roman count of a pregnancy: ten lunar months, not nine. pia iura parentum are the claims that pietas creates between parent and child, and the phrase looks both ways — what a parent is owed and what a parent owes.

sentences.t:
O utinam primis arsisses ignibus infans,
idque ego passa forem! Vixisti munere nostro:
sentences.l: Oh, if only you had burned as an infant in those first fires, and I had allowed it! You have lived by my gift:
sentences.i: If only you had burned as a baby in that first fire, and I had let it happen! You lived by my giving;
sentences.n: utinam with the pluperfect subjunctive arsisses is a wish for what can no longer be — the unattainable past. passa forem is an alternative form of passa essem, from the deponent patior, active in meaning: “and I had allowed it”. The colon at the line-end holds the balance open until 503.

sentences.t:
nunc merito moriere tuo. Cape praemia facti
bisque datam, primum partu, mox stipite rapto,
redde animam — vel me fraternis adde sepulcris!
sentences.l: now you shall die by your own deserving. Take the rewards of your deed, and give back the life given twice — first at the birth, then with the brand snatched away — or else add me to my brothers' graves!
sentences.i: now you will die by your own earning. Take the reward of what you did, and give back the life I gave you twice, first in bearing you and then in snatching the brand from the fire — or else lay me in my brothers' grave!
sentences.n: munere nostro set against merito tuo is the pivot the whole speech turns on: my gift, your desert. moriere is the second-singular future of the deponent morior, with the older ending -re for -ris. stipite rapto is an ablative with a participle standing parallel to the plain ablative partu, “first by the bearing, then by the brand snatched away”, and it points back to 456–457, when she pulled the brand out of the fire. praemia facti is bitter — the reward of the deed is the death.

sentences.t:
Et cupio et nequeo. Quid agam? modo vulnera fratrum
ante oculos mihi sunt et tantae caedis imago,
nunc animum pietas maternaque nomina frangunt. —
sentences.l: I both want to and cannot. What am I to do? At one moment my brothers' wounds are before my eyes and the picture of so great a killing; at the next, family love and a mother's names break my spirit. —
sentences.i: I want to and I cannot. What am I to do? One moment my brothers' wounds are in front of my eyes, and the sight of that great slaughter; the next, family love and the name of mother break me.
sentences.n: quid agam is a deliberative subjunctive, “what am I to do?”. modo ... nunc is the same swinging alternation as modo ... modo at 467. materna nomina picks up the two nomina of 464 — the pair that were dragging one heart — and this time the mother's name is pulling harder.

sentences.t:
Me miseram! male vincetis, sed vincite, fratres:
dummodo quae dedero vobis solacia vosque
sentences.l: Wretched me! you will conquer to my hurt — but conquer, my brothers — provided only that what consolations I shall have given you, and you as well,
sentences.i: Wretched that I am! Yours will be a cruel victory — but win it, brothers — provided only that the comfort I shall have given you, and you yourselves,
sentences.n: me miseram is an accusative of exclamation, a cry standing on its own with no verb. male vincetis does not mean the victory will fail: male here is “to my hurt”, so “you will win, and it will be an evil winning”. dedero is a future perfect — the giving is still to come. The solacia owed to the dead are exactly the vengeance she is about to take. The verb of her own clause, ipsa sequar, is held over into the next line.

sentences.t:
ipsa sequar.” Dixit, dextraque aversa trementi
funereum torrem medios coniecit in ignes.
sentences.l: I myself follow.” She spoke, and, turned away, with trembling right hand she hurled the funeral brand into the middle of the fire.
sentences.i: I shall follow myself.” She spoke, and with her face turned away she flung the death-bearing brand from her shaking hand into the heart of the fire.
sentences.n: aversa is nominative and agrees with her: she looks away as she throws. dextra trementi is an ablative of means. medios in ignes uses the Latin idiom by which the adjective marks the middle part of a thing — “into the middle of the fire”, not “into the middle fires”.

sentences.t:
Aut dedit aut visus gemitus est ipse dedisse
stipes, ut invitis correptus ab ignibus arsit.
sentences.l: Either the log itself gave a groan, or it seemed to have given one, as, caught by unwilling fires, it burned.
sentences.i: The log either groaned or seemed to groan as it caught and burned in fires that took it unwillingly.
sentences.n: aut ... aut leaves the marvel open, a way of reporting a portent without vouching for it. visus est ... dedisse is the personal use of videor with an infinitive, “it seemed to have given”. invitis ab ignibus is an ablative of agent with a personified fire: the flames are unwilling, and the reluctance in the scene has been moved onto them.

sentences.t:
Inscius atque absens flamma Meleagros ab illa
uritur et caecis torreri viscera sentit
ignibus ac magnos superat virtute dolores.
sentences.l: Unknowing and far away, Meleager is burned by that flame, and feels his vitals being scorched by unseen fires, and overcomes great pains by courage.
sentences.i: Meleager, who knew nothing of it and was nowhere near, was burning from that flame; he felt his insides being scorched by fires he could not see, and mastered the great pain by sheer courage.
sentences.n: Meleagros keeps the Greek nominative ending, and this is the first place in this part where he is named at all: he has been Oenides at 414, vulneris auctor at 418 and Mavortius at 437. sentit viscera torreri is an accusative and infinitive after a verb of perceiving, with viscera as the subject of the passive infinitive. caecis ignibus are fires that cannot be seen — caecus works in both directions in Latin, of what cannot see and of what cannot be seen.

sentences.t:
Quod tamen ignavo cadat et sine sanguine leto,
maeret et Ancaei felicia vulnera dicit
sentences.l: That he falls, though, by an inglorious death and without blood, he grieves at, and calls Ancaeus' wounds fortunate,
sentences.i: What grieves him, though, is that he is dying an inglorious death with no blood shed; he calls Ancaeus' wounds fortunate,
sentences.n: quod ... cadat is a substantival quod-clause serving as the object of maeret, “he grieves at the fact that ...”, and the subjunctive marks it as the ground he gives rather than a plain statement. leto is an ablative of the means of death. Ancaeus, whose rashness Theseus held up as a warning at 407, is named again here for his wounds; Meleager, dying with no mark on him, calls them fortunate — the death worth having is the bloody one.

sentences.t:
grandaevumque patrem fratresque piasque sorores
cum gemitu sociamque tori vocat ore supremo,
sentences.l: and his aged father and brothers and dutiful sisters and the partner of his bed he calls, with a groan, with his last mouth,
sentences.i: and with a groan he names, in his last words, his aged father, his brothers, his loyal sisters, the partner of his bed —
sentences.n: ore supremo, “with his last mouth”, is the Latin for a dying man's final words. socia tori, “partner of the couch”, is a periphrasis for his wife. The objects are strung on -que ... -que ... -que, the epic doubling that keeps a list moving inside the hexameter.

sentences.t:
forsitan et matrem. Crescunt ignisque dolorque
languescuntque iterum: simul est exstinctus uterque,
inque leves abiit paulatim spiritus auras
paulatim cana prunam velante favilla.
sentences.l: and perhaps his mother too. The fire and the pain grow and grow faint again: both were put out at the same moment, and little by little his breath went off into the thin air, little by little, with the white ash veiling the ember.
sentences.i: and perhaps his mother too. Fire and pain rose together and sank together; both went out at the same instant, and little by little his breath passed away into the thin air, little by little, as the grey ash covered the ember over.
sentences.n: forsitan et matrem is held back to the very end of the sentence and is the whole tragedy in three words: he may or may not have called on the woman who is killing him. exstinctus is the word for a fire going out and for a life ending, and here it does both at once. cana velante favilla is an ablative absolute; favilla is the fine ash that settles over a dying coal. The repeated paulatim across the line-break matches the two slow processes to each other.

sentences.t:
Alta iacet Calydon: lugent iuvenesque senesque,
vulgusque proceresque gemunt, scissaeque capillos
planguntur matres Calydonides Eueninae.
sentences.l: High Calydon lies low: young men and old alike mourn, commons and nobles alike groan, and, rent as to their hair, the Calydonian mothers of the Evenus beat themselves.
sentences.i: Lofty Calydon lies fallen. Young and old mourn together, commons and nobles groan together, and the mothers of Calydon by the Evenus tear their hair and beat their breasts.
sentences.n: alta iacet is a deliberate contradiction — the high city lies flat, and iaceo is the verb used of the fallen. scissae capillos is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle, “torn as to their hair”: a Greek construction Latin verse borrows, worth recognising because it looks like an impossible object on a passive verb. planguntur is the same voice in a finite verb, passive in form and reflexive in force, “they beat themselves”. Eueninae places them by the Evenus, the river of that country.

sentences.t:
Pulvere canitiem genitor vultusque seniles
foedat humi fusus spatiosumque increpat aevum.
sentences.l: The father fouls his white hair and his aged face with dust, poured out on the ground, and rails at his own long span of years.
sentences.i: His father lies stretched on the ground, defiling his white hair and old face with dust, and cursing the length of years he has been given.
sentences.n: humi is a locative, “on the ground”. canitiem, “whiteness”, stands for the white hair itself, the abstract used for the concrete. increpat is the verb for scolding aloud, and what he scolds is spatiosum aevum, the long life that has lasted into this.

sentences.t:
Nam de matre manus diri sibi conscia facti
exegit poenas acto per viscera ferro.
sentences.l: For from the mother her hand, knowing along with itself the dreadful deed, exacted the penalty with steel driven through her vitals.
sentences.i: For her own hand, conscious of the dreadful thing it had done, exacted the penalty from the mother, driving a blade through her body.
sentences.n: poenas exigere de aliquo is the idiom for exacting a penalty from someone, so de matre goes with exegit poenas: the penalty is exacted from her. sibi conscia is the ordinary Latin for a guilty conscience, literally “knowing along with itself”; the hand and not the woman is made the subject, so that the hand punishes what the hand did and the mother is what it punishes. acto per viscera ferro is an ablative absolute, and viscera makes its third appearance — hers at 478, his at 516, hers again here.

sentences.t:
Non mihi si centum deus ora sonantia linguis
ingeniumque capax totumque Helicona dedisset,
tristia persequerer miserarum dicta sororum.
sentences.l: Not, if a god had given me a hundred mouths sounding with tongues and a capacious genius and the whole of Helicon, would I get through the sad words of the wretched sisters.
sentences.i: Not if some god had given me a hundred mouths loud with tongues, a mind wide enough, and the whole of Helicon, could I follow to the end the sorrowful words of those poor sisters.
sentences.n: An unreal condition: pluperfect subjunctive dedisset in the if-clause, imperfect subjunctive persequerer in the main clause — a thing that did not happen, and a result that therefore cannot follow. The hundred mouths are the epic poet's standing confession that a subject is past telling. Helicon is the Muses' mountain in Boeotia, and the whole of it means all the poetry there is; Helicona keeps the Greek accusative ending. Magnus prints dicta, the sisters' words; some editions print fata, their fates.

sentences.t:
Inmemores decoris liventia pectora tundunt,
dumque manet corpus, corpus refoventque foventque,
oscula dant ipsi, posito dant oscula lecto.
sentences.l: Forgetful of what is seemly they beat their livid breasts, and while the body remains they chafe the body and chafe it again; they give kisses to him himself, they give kisses to the bier once it is laid out.
sentences.i: With no thought for decorum they beat their breasts black, and while the body is still with them they chafe it warm and chafe it again; they kiss him, and they kiss the couch itself once it is set out.
sentences.n: liventia is proleptic — the breasts are not livid until the beating makes them so, and the adjective states the result before the verb that causes it. refoventque foventque puts the compound before the simple verb, so that the repeated action seems to have no end. posito lecto is a dative with dant, answering ipsi in the first half of the line — kisses to him, then kisses to the couch — with the participle agreeing with lecto; the lectus is the couch on which a body was laid out for viewing.

sentences.t:
Post cinerem cineres haustos ad pectora pressant,
adfusaeque iacent tumulo signataque saxo
nomina complexae lacrimas in nomina fundunt.
sentences.l: After the ash they press the scooped-up ashes to their breasts, and, having poured themselves down upon the mound, they lie there, and, having embraced the names cut in the stone, they pour their tears upon the names.
sentences.i: When he was ashes, they gathered the ashes up and pressed them to their breasts; they threw themselves down on the mound and lay there, and clasped the names carved in the stone and poured their tears over the names.
sentences.n: post cinerem, “after the ash”, dates the scene after the cremation, and the singular cinerem is set against the plural cineres they gather up. adfusae is a middle-passive participle used reflexively, “having poured themselves down”, the same voice as planguntur at 528. nomina opens 541 in enjambement after signata ... saxo, then comes a second time inside the same line: what is left of him is a name, and they weep on it.

sentences.t:
Quas Parthaoniae tandem Latonia clade
exsatiata domus praeter Gorgenque nurumque
nobilis Alcmenae natis in corpore pennis
adlevat et longas per bracchia porrigit alas
corneaque ora facit versasque per aera mittit.
sentences.l: And them at last the daughter of Latona, glutted with the ruin of the house of Parthaon, all but Gorge and the daughter-in-law of noble Alcmena, lifts up, feathers having grown on their bodies, and stretches long wings along their arms, and makes their faces horny, and sends them, turned, through the air.
sentences.i: At last Latona's daughter, glutted with the ruin of Parthaon's house, raised them up on feathers that grew over their bodies — all but Gorge and noble Alcmena's daughter-in-law — spread long wings down their arms, gave them beaks of horn, and sent them off transformed through the air.
sentences.n: Quas is a connecting relative, “and them”, the last of several in this part (see 409 and 447). Latonia, “the daughter of Latona”, is Diana, and exsatiata says the ruin has at last been enough for her. Parthaon is the father of Oeneus, so the house of Parthaon is Meleager's on his father's side. The daughter-in-law of Alcmena is Deianira, wife of Alcmena's son Hercules. natis in corpore pennis is an ablative absolute; versas agrees with Quas, so the sisters are already changed when they are sent off.
